Rambling Intro - Honestly, Just Skip It

Most of us like to Game, and of those of us that like to Game, we'd probably prefer to be able to Game on an Operating System which does only what we tell it to do, and respects our privacy. So with that said, why is Windows still so fucking popular?

That was rhetorical by the way, the number one reason is pretty clear. Lack of Games - specifically, lack of the games that we want to play. Gaming on Linux has improved immensely over the past few years, with thousands of titles now available natively, but even with how much things have improved, the fact remains, the majority of Gamers migrating to Linux, from Windows, will be unable to take 100% of the games they like to play with them, using only native gaming.

So what's a possible solution: Throw the games away; learn to find a new found appreciation for crappy visual novels; or perhaps, dirty our hands with that often forbidden subject in the Linux Gaming world: Wine...

Native gaming is preferable, but in reality, not every PC game released will find its way onto Linux. At best, we can hope for a porting house like Feral Interactive to port some of the more popular triple-A titles, and there is always the Linux enthusiastic Indie developers to tide us over, but even so, that still leaves thousands of older games unlikely to ever see a Linux release, and if we still want to play them, without resorting to a VM, then Wine can be a viable alternative, depending on the Game.

So, enough rambling. This post aims to be a central, introductory sticky to Gaming with Wine on Linux, with Links to various other Voat posts on different topics, as well as links to external resources for additional reference and support.

Yes, this is interesting. I'd like to know how the subjects were primed on the stimulus. It makes a major difference if they clearly explain the nature of electric shock, and that it is painful, to the children. If not, then we could just be dealing with natural human curiosity. In a room of zero other stimuli, it's going to be pretty natural for someone to explore the only other interesting object in the room, with the interest level compounded by the fact the object is novel to them.

I consider myself a fairly intelligent person. As a grown adult I've played the game where you let a match burn in your finger tips as long as you can hold out. There is some base kind of satisfaction in testing our pain levels, in seeing what we can endure. In a context with zero other stimulation, it doesn't surprise me at all.

Again, that all depends on the intensity of the shock and how the children were primed. If they weren't explained to that there would be a shock, then they were just trapped. If they were, and the shock was intense, then this seems pretty irrational and the effect is more significant. If the shock was explained to them but was not a painful shock, then it just becomes a band-aid for boredom.

Hell, as a child, we used to play the human chain game with electric fences because electricity is fascinating and playing around with pain is a phenomenon that turns up in all sorts of human behaviors.
